design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person sleep-laboratory study with counterbalanced session order (incomplete 12-sequence Latin square): 7 adults with recent recreational MDMA use each completed three 3-night sessions, receiving on the treatment night MDMA with a full night in bed, placebo with a full night in bed, or placebo with a restricted night in bed (a positive control for sleep loss), followed by a placebo recovery night. Overnight polysomnography and next-day multiple sleep latency tests. A separate comparison set the participants' first laboratory night and placebo-day sleepiness tests against 13 age-matched people without drug use drawn from a general-population sleep study.
can_establish: Within these 7 people, how MDMA compared with placebo changes polysomnographic sleep that night and the next night, and whether next-day objective sleepiness after MDMA resembles that after placebo or after a night of restricted sleep.
cannot_establish: Effects of MDMA at other doses, taken at parties with dancing, heat, other drugs or no sleep opportunity; effects after repeated use; whether next-day sleepiness after MDMA truly differs from either comparison (it differed from neither, in 7 people); and whether the differences between the MDMA group and the controls were caused by MDMA (cross-sectional, different recruitment and schedules).

sample.recruitment: Public advertisements (MDMA group); comparison group selected from a concurrent southeastern Michigan general-population study of sleep and daytime sleepiness.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 18 to 35; at least high-school education; weight under 91 kg; at least 6 lifetime uses of recreational stimulants including at least 3 recent MDMA uses, one in the past 6 months; no current or past Axis I disorder including drug or alcohol dependence (other than nicotine), abuse allowed if in remission for a year; no more than 100 MDMA uses or 50 uses of stimulants, opioids, phencyclidine or sedatives; not pregnant or lactating. Comparison group: no illicit drug use history, no shift work, sleep disorder, serious illness, substance abuse or psychiatric diagnosis.
sample.demographics: MDMA group: 5 white men, 1 white woman, 1 African American woman; age 19 to 34 (mean 25.3); lifetime MDMA uses mean 27 (range 3 to 75); cannabis 6 of 7, cocaine 1, other stimulants 2, other hallucinogens 2. Usual home schedule (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index): late bedtime and late rising, 7.8 hours of sleep, 17 minutes to fall asleep, Epworth score 6.8. Comparison group: 10 men and 3 women, age-matched.
sample.attrition: Two further participants withdrew (one after the restricted-sleep session; one after the placebo and MDMA sessions) and are not analysed; three planned participants could not be recruited, leaving the Latin square incomplete.
sample.selection_effects: Light-to-moderate MDMA experience (mean 27 uses, against 112 in an earlier study the authors cite), screened free of psychiatric disorders and dependence; the laboratory bedtime was much earlier than the participants' usual one, which the authors note may have lengthened sleep onset in all conditions.

exposure.measurement: Doses given by the investigators under double-blind conditions in a supervised sleep laboratory; urine drug screens and breathalyser negative at the start of every session.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: racemic MDMA hydrochloride (from David Nichols, Purdue University) 2 mg/kg by salt weight, by mouth in a gelatin capsule filled with dextrose, at 18:00 on the treatment night (night 2); identical dextrose placebo capsules otherwise. Time in bed 23:00 to 07:00 (8 hours) on placebo and MDMA nights; 03:00 to 07:00 (4 hours) with placebo on the restricted-sleep night; placebo at 18:00 and 8 hours in bed on the recovery night (night 3). Multiple sleep latency tests at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00 on days 2 and 3. Sessions at least 1 week apart. Participants agreed not to use illicit drugs between sessions, cannabis for 2 days and alcohol for 12 hours before sessions; usual coffee and tobacco allowed at breaks at least 1 hour before each nap test.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis (6 of 7) and other drug use history recorded; abstinence before sessions instructed and checked by urine screens (people who used cannabis regularly were tested on the 2 days before and the day of each session).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Negative urine drug screen and breathalyser at the start of each session; supervised throughout sessions.

comparison.controls: Each participant's own placebo session (a full night in bed) and restricted-sleep session (placebo, a shortened night in bed; exposure field). Separately, 13 age-matched people without illicit drug use, recorded on a single night and next day with no capsule.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparisons with counterbalanced order; the comparison group was matched on age only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep before any MDMA use is unknown; the authors note it would be important to know whether the disturbances in the MDMA group predated stimulant use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group had no illicit drug use; the MDMA group's cannabis and other drug use is a confounder for the between-group comparison.

outcomes.instruments: Nocturnal polysomnography (central and occipital EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG; Rechtschaffen and Kales scoring by experienced scorers with 90% reliability): total sleep time, latency to persistent sleep, wake after persistent sleep, percentages of stages 1, 2, 3/4 and REM, REM latency. Multiple sleep latency test (four naps): mean sleep latency and sleep-onset REM periods.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard, validated sleep measures; the comparison group's values matched published norms according to the authors.
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disruption as shorter total sleep, longer sleep latency and shifts in stage percentages; next-day sleepiness as a shorter mean sleep latency on the nap tests.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (eight polysomnographic and two nap-test measures, each in several analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not stated for the scorers; drug administration double-blind (the restricted-sleep condition cannot be blinded).

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures general linear models (mean and SEM reported). MDMA against placebo over treatment and recovery nights (df 1 and 6): total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes on the treatment night, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, drug by night interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003 (reduced on the treatment night only); stage 2 P = 0.267, stage 3/4 P = 0.119, REM latency P = 0.589, wake after sleep onset not significant. Treatment nights of all three conditions (df 2 and 12): total sleep F = 17.272 (printed P = 0.005); REM F = 15.036, P = 0.001. Next-day nap tests: treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; condition means only in a figure. MDMA group against comparison group (df 18): first-night total sleep 376.21 (26.7) against 433.43 (13.1) minutes, t = 2.59; stage 3/4 4.8 (0.7)% against 15.7 (3.4)%, t = 2.90; placebo-day mean nap latency 15.6 (1.76) against 10.9 (4.39) minutes, t = 2.84. Editors' arithmetic: MDMA shortened sleep on the treatment night by about 126 minutes, restricted sleep by about 218 minutes.
analysis.selective_reporting: All polysomnographic measures are tabulated; nap-test values by condition are given only in a figure.
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors call the study preliminary and name the small sample as a limitation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: MDMA on the treatment night, compared with placebo, cut total sleep by about two hours, mainly by delaying sleep onset, raised light (stage 1) sleep and almost abolished REM sleep (3.5% against 19.2%), with sleep back to placebo levels on the next night. Next-day sleepiness after MDMA did not differ from placebo, but it did not differ from restricted sleep either; restricted sleep made people sleepier than placebo. Against 13 people without drug use, the MDMA group's first laboratory night was shorter with much less slow-wave sleep, and their nap latencies were longer, with more sleep-onset REM periods.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says acute MDMA "reduced stage 3/4 sleep", that MDMA-related sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness, and that people in the MDMA group showed hyperarousal and impaired REM function, likely due to the deleterious effects of MDMA on catecholamines. Gaps: (1) the drug comparison found no effect on stage 3/4 (P = 0.119); the stage 3/4 difference is between the MDMA group and the comparison group; (2) 'not associated with sleepiness' rests on a non-difference in 7 people from a condition that also did not differ from sleep restriction; (3) hyperarousal, impaired REM function and a catecholamine mechanism are inferred from a cross-sectional comparison with a differently recruited group on a different schedule, which cannot show that MDMA caused the differences, as the authors partly concede.

timeline.event: This preliminary study; the authors describe their results as consistent with an earlier placebo-controlled study by McCann et al. showing sleep disruption with MDMA (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The only placebo-controlled polysomnographic study of MDMA and next-day sleepiness read for the library; its next-night findings are large and plausible but rest on 7 people, and the next-day sleepiness question is unresolved.

funding.declared_conflicts: Not an industry-supported study. Johanson is an employee of CRS Associates LLC, a for-profit consulting company; the other authors report no financial conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Wayne State University and Henry Ford Hospital sleep researchers (Roehrs); the laboratory was at Detroit Receiving Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A larger placebo-controlled crossover study of MDMA at doses and times people actually use, with polysomnography, next-day nap tests and performance and mood measures over the following days, people's own sleep schedules respected, and a pre-registered analysis.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Counterbalanced with a 12-sequence Latin square, of which only 7 sequences were completed; order effects cannot be fully balanced.
Sessions at least a week apart, each beginning with a baseline night; baseline nights did not differ between conditions.
MDMA against placebo was double-blind, but MDMA's effects are noticeable and blinding was not checked; the restricted-sleep condition was necessarily unblinded.
Two of nine who began withdrew and were excluded, one of them after the placebo and MDMA sessions.
Objective polysomnography and nap tests scored by experienced scorers to standard criteria; scorer blinding is not stated, but these measures leave little room for interpretation.
No registration; the abstract reports a stage 3/4 effect the results do not show, and nap-test values appear only in a figure.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns in four domains, none high; the outcomes are objective, and the large REM and total-sleep effects are unlikely to be artefacts of order or blinding. The between-group comparison with people without drug use is observational and not covered by RoB 2: it is confounded by recruitment source, cannabis and other drug use, sex mix, habitual late sleep schedules and the number of laboratory nights, and should not be cited as an effect of MDMA. May be cited for the treatment-night and recovery-night sleep effects of a single laboratory dose in 7 experienced adults, and for the unresolved next-day sleepiness comparison.

key_findings.finding: Seven adults with recreational MDMA experience completed all three sessions (5 white men, 1 white woman, 1 African American woman; mean age 25.3; lifetime MDMA uses mean 27, range 3 to 75); two others withdrew and three planned participants could not be recruited.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Experimental Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results › Demographics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Treatment night, MDMA against placebo: total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes (F(1,6) = 8.6, P = 0.026), latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes (F = 7.0, P = 0.038), stage 1 sleep 8.4 against 6.6% (F = 9.49, P = 0.022); no significant effect on wake after sleep onset, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: REM sleep was 3.5% (SEM 2.1) of sleep on the MDMA night against 19.2% (2.0) on the placebo night (F(1,6) = 14.28, P = 0.009), reduced on the treatment night only (drug by night interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); it was also lower than after restricted sleep (19.3%; post hoc P = 0.004), so the authors read it as a specific REM-suppressing effect rather than a result of sleep loss.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: On the placebo recovery night after the MDMA session, total sleep was 403.6 (34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), close to the recovery night of the placebo session (431.9 minutes; 20.6%); apart from REM, no main effects of night or night-by-drug interactions were found.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3, recovery column

key_findings.finding: Next-day objective sleepiness: a treatment by day interaction (F(2,12) = 4.63, P = 0.032); after restricted sleep, mean sleep latency on the nap tests was shorter than after placebo (falling to about 6 minutes), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from restricted sleep; on the following day the three conditions did not differ. Sleep-onset REM periods: 2.14 after restricted sleep, 1.43 after MDMA and 1.00 after placebo, not significantly different.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Compared with 13 age-matched people without drug use, the MDMA group's first laboratory night had less total sleep (376.21, SEM 26.7, against 433.43, 13.1, minutes; t = 2.59, df 18, P < 0.02) and less stage 3/4 sleep (4.8% against 15.7%; t = 2.90, P < 0.01), with similar REM; on the placebo day their mean nap latency was longer (15.6 against 10.9 minutes; t = 2.84, P < .01) and they had more sleep-onset REM periods (5 of 7 had at least one).
key_findings.locator: Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects; Results › Effects on the MSLT, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors name the small sample and the laboratory schedule, which was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times, as limitations, and say it would be important to know whether the disturbances in the MDMA group predated stimulant use.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says acute MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, but the results report no effect of MDMA on the stage 3/4 percentage (P = 0.119; Table 3: 5.0% against 5.7% on the treatment night); the reduced stage 3/4 sleep is in the comparison between the MDMA group and people without drug use.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Measurements and Results; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Reduced slow-wave sleep should not be cited as an acute effect of MDMA from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The post-hoc P values for total sleep conflict: the text gives MDMA against placebo P = 0.031 and MDMA against restricted sleep P = 0.093, while the Figure 2 legend gives restricted sleep against placebo P = 0.031 and MDMA against placebo P = 0.001.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The exact significance of the MDMA effect on total sleep in the three-way comparison is uncertain; the two-factor analysis (P = 0.026) is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: F = 17.272 with df 2 and 12 is printed with P = 0.005, and F = 15.036 with P = 0.001; the editors' calculation gives p of about 0.0003 and 0.0005.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both effects are significant either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-group t of 2.59 for total sleep cannot be reproduced from the printed values (editors' calculation: about 1.9 to 2.2 if the spreads are SEMs, as in Table 3, and about 6.5 if they are SDs), while the nap-latency t of 2.84 roughly fits the values only if they are SDs; the paper does not say which.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects; Results › Effects on the MSLT, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-group statistics cannot be checked; treat their significance as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group's mean number of sleep-onset REM periods is printed as 0.008 (SD 0.28), which is impossible for 13 people (the smallest possible non-zero mean is about 0.08); the printed t of 4.51 is reproduced only with 0.008 (editors' calculation; with 0.08, t is about 4.2). The MDMA group's placebo-day value is given as 1.00 with a spread of 0.82 in one paragraph and 0.71 in the next.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical or calculation errors; the conclusion (more sleep-onset REM periods in the MDMA group) holds either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 3 footnote says the data came from a general-population database of Michigan residents, which describes the comparison group, not the MDMA-group data in Table 3; and the text says values 'may differ from Table 1', which holds drug-exposure data (Table 3 seems meant).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 footnote; Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects
reporting_issues.consequence: Editorial errors that obscure which data come from which group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 3 legend reports a main effect of night on REM percentage (P = 0.001), while the text says there were no main effects of night apart from the REM interaction.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figure 3 legend; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the REM analysis.
